title: How to handle illustrator to after effects asset preparation on Mac for 2026 projects
metaTitle: Illustrator to After Effects: Asset Preparation Guide for Mac
description: Learn how to prepare your illustration files for animation in After Effects. Avoid common pitfalls, save hours of rework, and keep your creative workflow steady.
intro: Preparing your files for motion is the bridge between static art and animation. When you move from illustrator to after effects, your file structure dictates whether the animation process is smooth or a total nightmare.
tldr: Always separate moving parts onto individual named layers.
Draw hidden areas behind joints to prevent gaps during rotation.
Consult with your animator before you start drawing to define movement needs.
Use consistent naming conventions for all layers and groups.
Avoid merging layers until the final export stage.

blocks.text: Why asset preparation for animation matters

When you draw for print, you focus on the final look. When you draw for animation, you must build for movement. Animation software like After Effects treats every layer as a separate object. If you draw an arm as one piece, you cannot rotate it at the elbow. You must split the arm into upper arm, forearm, and hand layers. This is the core of asset preparation.

Many illustrators assume the animator can just cut up their artwork. This is a mistake. The animator does not have your original brushes or layer styles. If they have to cut your art, they will inevitably distort your lines. Your art quality will drop. Proper preparation means you retain control over how your work looks in motion.
Common causes of animation file failure

items: Merging layers too early in the creative process.
Using generic layer names like Layer 1, Layer 2, or Copy 3.
Drawing only the visible parts of an object without accounting for rotation.
Failing to communicate with the animator about which parts need to move.
Ignoring the need for overlapping joints to prevent visual gaps.

blocks.text: You do not need expensive plugins to fix your workflow. Start by talking to your animator. Ask them exactly what needs to move. If you are the animator, sketch out the rig on paper before you touch your Mac. Use a naming convention like body_part_side_segment. For example, use arm_left_upper instead of arm1.

Always draw full shapes. If an eye is behind an eyelid, draw the whole eye. When the eyelid moves, the full eye will be there. You will never see a white gap or a jagged edge. This simple habit saves hours of patching up files during the animation phase.

When you are deep in Photoshop or Illustrator, you do not want to break your focus to look up shortcuts or file settings. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur where a setting is. Lazur will point at the menu item or panel you need. This keeps your hands on your tablet and your eyes on your canvas.

Creative work is draining. The cognitive load of managing complex layer structures adds to your stress. Schedule your asset preparation for your lower energy hours. Save your sharpest morning hours for the actual illustration. Use your afternoon slump to organize, name, and group your layers.

faq.question: Should I use vector or raster for animation?
faq.answer: It depends on the style. Vectors are better for clean, crisp motion and scaling. Raster is better for textured, painterly styles. Most workflows use both.

faq.question: How do I know what to separate into layers?
faq.answer: Anything that needs to move independently or rotate needs its own layer. Think of your character like a paper doll with joints.

faq.question: Is asset preparation billable time?
faq.answer: Yes. You should include it in your project estimate as part of your production time. Do not treat it as free work.

costs.title: Lost Billable Hours
costs.text: Rebuilding files because of poor layering costs you time you could spend on new projects.

costs.title: Creative Quality Degradation
costs.text: When animators have to cut up your work, they often distort your original brush strokes and line quality.

costs.title: Project Delays
costs.text: Technical issues during the animation phase often push back delivery dates and damage client trust.

causes.title: Lack of Communication
causes.text: Not asking the animator about their rig requirements before you start drawing.

causes.title: Production Habits
causes.text: Treating animation files like static print files where layers are merged or flattened.

causes.title: Underestimating Complexity
causes.text: Assuming that simple movements do not require careful joint and hidden area planning.

fixes.title: Layering Strategy
fixes.text: Put every moving part on its own named layer. Use clear, descriptive names for every group.

fixes.title: Joint Overlap
fixes.text: Extend your art at joints like elbows and knees to prevent gaps during rotation.

fixes.title: Complete Hidden Areas
fixes.text: Draw the full shape of objects even if they are partially obscured by other parts.
